title: Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - Anti-Competitive Practices
subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: An agreement among competitors to divide a market by allocating customers or geographic territories among themselves is an illegal practice known as:
questions.explain: Market Division or Allocation schemes occur when competing firms agree to divide specific customers, products, or territories amongst themselves rather than competing for them.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Three local paving contractors meet secretly and agree that Contractor A will be the low bidder on Project 1, Contractor B on Project 2, and Contractor C on Project 3. This specific scheme is called:
questions.explain: Bid rotation is a form of bid-rigging where competitors agree to take turns being the winning (lowest) bidder on a series of contracts.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: To ensure Contractor A wins a bid, Contractors B and C submit bids that are intentionally too high to be competitive or contain unacceptable terms. What type of bid-rigging are B and C participating in?
questions.explain: Complementary bidding (also known as 'cover bidding' or 'courtesy bidding') occurs when competitors submit token bids that are intentionally designed to fail to give the appearance of genuine competition.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: A buyer is reviewing five submitted bids and notices that three different vendors have the exact same mathematical miscalculation in their pricing sheet, and all three submissions use identical font and formatting. This is a primary red flag for:
questions.explain: Identical typos, formatting, or bizarre identical mathematical errors across bids from supposedly independent companies are strong red flags indicating that the vendors colluded in preparing their bids.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: The core federal statute in the United States that outlaws combinations, contracts, or conspiracies in restraint of trade (such as price-fixing and bid-rigging) is the:
questions.explain: The Sherman Antitrust Act is the fundamental federal law prohibiting anti-competitive practices like price-fixing and bid-rigging that restrain interstate trade.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Competitors agreeing to establish a standard minimum fee or a standard formula for determining prices is known as:
questions.explain: Price-fixing involves an agreement among competitors to raise, fix, or otherwise maintain the price at which their goods or services are sold.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: If a procurement official suspects that vendors are engaging in bid-rigging, what is the most appropriate first course of action?
options: Immediately cancel the solicitation and publicly accuse the vendors.
Notify legal counsel and follow agency procedures for reporting anti-competitive behavior.
Call the vendors individually and ask if they colluded.
Award the contract to the lowest bidder and investigate post-award.
questions.explain: Procurement officials should never confront suspects directly as it may destroy evidence. The proper action is to notify the agency's legal counsel or appropriate investigatory authority (e.g., Inspector General) and follow internal reporting procedures.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Four regional suppliers of chlorine gas meet at a trade association event and agree not to sell to agencies outside their traditional zip codes. This prevents them from competing against one another. This is an example of:
questions.explain: This is a geographic market allocation scheme, a severe antitrust violation where competitors agree to stay out of each other's territories, creating miniature monopolies in each area.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Vendor A tells Vendor B: 'If you do not submit a bid for the downtown road project, I will hire your firm as a lucrative subcontractor once I win it.' Vendor B agrees and withdraws their bid. This is known as:
questions.explain: Bid suppression occurs when one or more competitors agree to refrain from bidding or agree to withdraw a previously submitted bid so that a designated competitor's bid will be accepted.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance
